units.title: Established alternative L1s
angles: Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

Faces. Find every way one balance at the PoolManager can be reached under two currency ids or in two units on this network (native asset with an ERC-20 face, wrapped native predeploys, bridged and canonical versions sharing storage, tokens with more than one entry point), and walk sync, settle, take, mint and burn across the two faces in every order.

units.title: OP Stack chains with ETH gas
angles: Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

Faces. Find every way one balance at the PoolManager can be reached under two currency ids or in two units on this network (native asset with an ERC-20 face, wrapped native predeploys, bridged and canonical versions sharing storage, tokens with more than one entry point), and walk sync, settle, take, mint and burn across the two faces in every order.

code.task: Answers lead L-318; report it in leadResults. The live PoolManagers hold years of logs, and any capture that has already happened leaves a trace whatever its cause. Search for them without assuming a mechanism. On each of the 21 networks, over as long a range as the endpoint or an explorer export serves: (a) list ERC-6909 Transfer events of the PoolManager from the zero address (claim mints; the event is Transfer(address caller, address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 indexed id, uint256 amount), see src/ERC6909.sol and src/interfaces/external/IERC6909Claims.sol for the exact signature) and keep those whose transaction contains no ERC-20 Transfer of that currency into the PoolManager, no native value sent to the PoolManager, and no swap or liquidity event that would explain a credit; (b) list transactions in which the PoolManager pays a token out and gets the same amount back around a call to a third contract, with the caller ending richer; (c) list transactions with a native take whose recipient is not the caller and that revert-free end with the caller's native credit unexplained; (d) list transactions where a take of currency X is followed by a settle of X of a larger amount without a matching Transfer in. For every class of hit, fetch a trace of one example (debug_traceTransaction where served, otherwise the explorer's internal transaction and log view), name the third contract and the function called between sync and settle, and decide whether the amount was unaccounted surplus or an accounted balance of a pool, position or claim holder. The sLGNS, sATH, sKLIMA and USDI cases of cycle 4 (F-066, F-067) and AMPL (F-041) are known; report what is new: other tokens, other networks, other third contracts, and above all any case where the PoolManager's balance of a currency afterwards is lower than pools and claims record. Keep scripts in your output directory, and keep raw downloads under a subdirectory named raw. Rank the hits by amount.

Answers leads L-319 and L-292; report both in leadResults. _settle credits the caller with the rise of balanceOf(PoolManager) since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365), and take pays out with a plain transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:60-80). The credit is counted in units of balanceOf; the payout is in freely transferable units. Find every pooled token on the 21 networks where these two differ or where a third party can move the reported balance. Part one: tokens that count locked, staked, vesting, frozen, escrowed or cooldown amounts in balanceOf and let another account assign such an amount to any holder (stakeFor, lockFor, transferWithLock, vestTo, depositFor with a hold period, airdrop with lock, bonded transfers, tokens with per-lot transfer restrictions such as ERC-1404, ERC-3643 and ERC-1400 partitions). For each, simulate read-only in one unlock: sync, assign a locked amount to the PoolManager, settle, take the same amount; does the take succeed and pay liquid units that other users deposited, leaving the PoolManager with locked ones? That would take or freeze accounted funds and is a high finding. Part two: tokens whose balanceOf an ordinary account can raise for the PoolManager and that later falls back: balances that follow a spot price or an oracle anyone can update, a share rate that a donation or a flash loan moves and that can be unwound in the same transaction, a rebase that reverses, a reward that is clawed back, a debt or negative rebase that lands later. Part three: other public triggers of a one-way increase (public rebase, accrue, harvest, distribute, claimFor, checkpoint, poke) beyond the tokens F-041, F-060, F-066 and F-067 already name, with the amount bookable today. Take token lists from research/network-risk/cycles/004/theme-balance-reconcile.work (the scripts and result files of the balance comparison; the raw downloads may be absent) and from explorer token holdings of each PoolManager, and search verified sources by function name. Give for each token the network, the pooled amount and its value, the function, who may call it, and the result of the simulation.

Answers leads L-258 and L-316; report both in leadResults. Anyone can initialize a pool that names any existing hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-143, src/libraries/Hooks.sol), and the hook is then called with the attacker's PoolKey, including two currencies the attacker wrote. Many pools of ordinary users share a few hook contracts. For each of the 21 networks, count hooks by number of initialized pools from the Initialize logs of the PoolManager (the hook is in the log data) and take the five most used, plus the hooks named in the leads on Robinhood Chain, Elysium, X Layer and Monad. For each: read the verified source or decompile; say which flags its address carries, above all the return delta flags; test with eth_call whether an ordinary account can initialize a new pool on it with currencies of its own; and establish whether its callbacks tell pools apart (by pool id, by currency, by a list of pools it created) before they touch state, funds or approvals that other pools rely on. Look for: storage keyed without the pool id; a hook that holds tokens, ERC-6909 claims or approvals for several pools and pays out according to arguments the caller controls; a hook that takes from or settles for the PoolManager on behalf of the pool given in the key; fee, oracle, cooldown or limit state that a foreign pool can write; hook functions other than the callbacks that anyone can call; a hook that trusts msg.sender == PoolManager and nothing else. A path by which an account that created its own pool on a shared hook takes funds of, or blocks, users of other pools on that hook is in scope with the hook named as the cause; say how much value the affected pools hold.

ERC-6909 claims are the PoolManager's own token (src/ERC6909.sol, src/ERC6909Claims.sol). burn(from, id, amount) and transferFrom spend an allowance or use operator rights (read the exact checks). For each of the 21 networks, list from the PoolManager's logs the addresses that appear as operator in OperatorSet events and as spender in Approval events, with the number of owners that approved each. For each such address read its code: does it run calls that any caller supplies (Multicall3, Across MulticallHandler, aggregator executors, relay forwarders, settlement contracts with user callbacks, EIP-7702 delegates with a public batch function, routers with an arbitrary call action), or expose a function through which any caller can make it call PoolManager.transferFrom or PoolManager.burn with a from address the caller chooses? If so, any account can move the claims of everyone who approved it: give the owners still holding claims, the ids and the amounts. Then the second question (lead from the cycle 4 critic): when one currency of a pool rejects transfers from the PoolManager (ViciCoin after its daily allowance is used, G$ on Celo, a paused wrapped stock token, a frozen TIP-20), can a position held through the deployed PositionManager of that network still be closed so that the other currency is paid out? Read the action list of the PositionManager from its verified source (take, take pair, mint 6909, clear or take, sweep) and say which sequence, if any, lets an ordinary liquidity provider leave with the other currency and a claim for the blocked one, and whether the front ends users rely on can produce it.
